entities.name: Bardo Thodol
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Bardo Thodol, often translated as 'The Tibetan Book of the Dead,' is a seminal text in Tibetan Buddhism that provides insights into the afterlife and the intermediate state between death and rebirth, known as the bardo. This text, attributed to the legendary Indian tantric master Padmasambhava, holds a significant place in the Nyingma school of Tibetan Buddhism, emerging in the 8th century CE against a backdrop of cultural exchange between India and Tibet. The work was revealed by the revered Tibetan treasure discoverer Karma Lingpa in the 14th century, marking a pivotal moment in the spiritual landscape of Tibetan Buddhism and influencing a multitude of practices and beliefs surrounding death and the afterlife.

The text is structured as a guide for the deceased, walking them through the phenomena they might encounter after death. It describes various stages of the bardo, emphasizing the importance of recognizing the illusory nature of these experiences to achieve liberation. The teachings encapsulated in the Bardo Thodol have transformed Tibetan funerary practices, where recitations of the text are performed to guide the departed soul, thus intertwining the text with the cultural and spiritual life of Tibetan communities.

The legacy of the Bardo Thodol extends beyond its immediate religious context; it has been a vital conduit for the transmission of Tibetan Buddhism into the global consciousness, particularly in the 20th century as Western interest in Eastern spirituality grew. This text has influenced not only Buddhist thought but has also permeated popular culture and contemporary discussions on death and consciousness. As the prominent Tibetan scholar Chögyam Trungpa noted, 'The Bardo Thodol teaches us to see the nature of mind and to realize our inherent potential for enlightenment.'
